title: Inquest jury into refugee's death calls for end to holding immigration detainees in jails
subtitle: Five jurors declined to declare Abdurahman Ibrahim Hassan's death a homicide, instead simply calling it a 'sudden death during struggle/restraint with a towel placed on the mouth, under the nose in the setting of schizophrenia and hypertensive heart disease.'
article: What caused Abdurahman Ibrahim Hassan 's death will remain a subject of debate.
But inquest jurors said Friday they hope his story can lead to something: an end to the practice of housing immigration detainees in Ontario jails.

After a day and a half of deliberation, the five jurors reviewing the death of Hassan , a refugee with a lengthy history of mental illness, delivered their verdict, making 53 recommendations - directed at federal and provincial authorities, police and correctional services, and Peterborough Regional Health Centre - to avoid similar deaths in the future.

Hassan, who came to Canada in 1992 and was granted asylum a year later, had had numerous run-ins with the law and was flagged for removal from this country as early as 2005. After serving a jail sentence for his last conviction, he was taken into Canada Border Services Agency custody in 2012 and detained at a maximum-security facility in Lindsay, Ont., pending deportation.

On June 3, 2015, the 39-year-old man was found to be unresponsive in a segregated cell there and taken to hospital for seizures. He died eight days later during a struggle in his bed under the guard of two paid-duty police officers, one of whom had a towel over Hassan's mouth to restrain him and stop him from smearing feces and spitting at others.

Advocates who were granted intervenor status at the inquest had urged the jury to rule Hassan's death a homicide, because the two police officers and nurses present in his room could have foreseen the risks of his death with the towel covering his mouth during the struggle.

However, the jury ultimately sided with the finding of Ontario's chief pathologist - and lawyers for the government, police and hospital officials - that the cause of death was inconclusive and that Hassan died of a "sudden death during struggle/restraint with a towel placed on the mouth, under the nose in the setting of schizophrenia and hypertensive heart disease."
Despite the verdict, the three community intervenors said they were pleased most of their proposed recommendations were adopted by the jury.

"It is clear that Mr. Hassan was a victim to multiple systems, including health care, and that his identity as a Black, mentally ill refugee contributed to his treatment here in Canada. Sadly, his experience in these carceral systems is not unique," said Nana Yanful, legal director of Black Legal Action Centre.
"We expect the recommendations will be used to initiate strong improvements to prevent another Mr. Hassan from dying in custody."
Added Aleks Selim Dughman-Manzur, president of the Canadian Council for Refugees, "The verdict sends a clear message that we must have a strong civilian oversight."

Both police officers involved in Hassan's death - Peterborough Police Const. Alicia McGriskin and now-deceased OPP Const. Andy Eberhardt - were cleared of any wrongdoing by Ontario's Special Investigations Unit, an oversight body for police conduct.
"The jury's cause of death statement and verdict completely exonerated PC Eberhardt, Constable McGriskin and the nurses," the Ontario Provincial Police Association said in a statement.

"It is important to recognize and acknowledge that during this incident PC Eberhardt and Constable McGriskin conducted themselves in the best traditions of the OPP and Peterborough Police Service, and Ontarians can be thankful for their service."

During the 17 days of witness testimony, the five-member jury heard how the federal detainee ended up in a provincial jail ; his conditions in detention over periods of segregation ; his physical- and mental-health challenges and treatment ; his behavioural changes in his final days; the restraints and care he received in the hospital ; and the immediate events leading up to his death at 1:28 a.m. on June 11, 2015.
Beside the call to end immigration detention in provincial jails, the jury also made recommendations directed at:

"The jury has delivered a powerful set of recommendations that if implemented will help bring an end to the mistreatment of immigration detainees with mental illnesses," said Andrew Brouwer, who represented the Refugee Law Office at the inquest.
"Now Canada and Ontario must take the necessary steps to prevent similar deaths of detainees in the future. The practice of jailing immigration detainees indefinitely must end."

Inquest jury recommendations are non-binding, and governments and other entities to which they are directed have no legal obligation to implement them. However, both Ontario's Ministry of the Solicitor General and the federal border agency said they will carefully review the recommendations.

"The CBSA will continue to improve conditions and reduce the ratio of detainees, while supporting the humane and dignified treatment of individuals in its care," said a spokesperson for the border agency.

The inquest has heard that to date four provinces - British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba and Nova Scotia - have given notice that they are going to stop holding immigration detainees in provincial jails when their agreements with the federal government expire.
